pages.text: Push a heavy box across a rough cement floor and you feel the floor pushing back. Ride a bicycle fast and you feel the air pressing against your chest. These are two forces that oppose motion. The first is friction, which acts wherever two surfaces rub together. The second is air resistance, which acts on anything moving through air. Both turn useful movement energy into heat. Rub your palms together quickly and you can feel that heat. Every car, lorry, and train burns extra fuel just to overcome these two forces.

pages.text: Friction is not always a nuisance. Without it your sandals would slip on the ground, tyres could not grip the road, and brakes could not stop a vehicle. But where we want things to move easily, we reduce friction. We put oil or grease between moving parts. We use wheels and ball bearings so that surfaces roll instead of slide. We make surfaces smooth. Air resistance is reduced by shape. A streamlined shape, narrow and smooth like a fish or a bird, lets air slide past. That is why fast trains and aeroplanes have pointed noses.

pages.text: What if a train never touched its track? Magnets make this possible. Every magnet has two poles, north and south. Like poles repel each other, and unlike poles attract. A maglev train (short for magnetic levitation) uses strong electromagnets to lift the whole train a few centimetres above the guideway. With no wheels on rails, there is almost no friction. Other magnets along the track pull the train forward from the front and push it from behind. In 2015, a test maglev train in Japan reached 603 km/h, the fastest any train has travelled.

pages.text: A maglev train still has to push through air. At high speed, air resistance becomes the biggest force of all. In 2013, the businessman Elon Musk published a design he called the hyperloop. Small passenger pods would float on magnets inside a long sealed tube with most of the air pumped out. With almost no friction and almost no air resistance, he suggested, a pod could travel at about 1,200 km/h, close to the speed of sound. The idea was not completely new. In 1867, visitors to an exhibition in New York rode in a carriage blown through a tube by air.

pages.text: Several companies tried to build it. One, called Hyperloop One, laid a 500-metre test tube in the desert of Nevada in the United States. In 2017, an empty pod reached 387 km/h there. In November 2020, two members of staff became the first passengers, travelling at 172 km/h. That was far below the promised speed, and slower than ordinary fast trains. The costs were enormous. Keeping hundreds of kilometres of tube almost empty of air, and safe for passengers, proved very difficult. At the end of 2023 the company closed. Research continues elsewhere, but no hyperloop carries passengers today.

pages.text: The science behind the hyperloop is sound. Less friction and less air resistance really do mean less wasted energy. But a good idea in physics is not yet a working machine. Engineers must also make it safe, reliable, and affordable. Still, the numbers are exciting. Accra to Kumasi is about 250 kilometres. By VIP or STC bus it often takes seven hours. At the speed of Japan’s maglev it would take 25 minutes. The same forces act on you every day. A cyclist who bends low over the handlebars meets less air resistance, and a well-oiled chain wastes less of the rider’s energy.

activities.question: What happens to the energy that friction takes away from a moving object?
Why does a maglev train have almost no friction with its track?
options: Its wheels are made of very smooth steel
Magnets lift it so that it does not touch the track
It travels too slowly for friction to act

activities.question: Why would pods inside a hyperloop tube meet very little air resistance?
options: The tube is filled with cold air
Most of the air has been pumped out of the tube

activities.question: Apply it: A grinding mill becomes hot and noisy, and its engine uses more fuel than before. What is the most likely cause, and the best first remedy?
options: Too little friction; add sand to the moving parts
Too much friction between moving parts; clean and oil them
Too much air resistance; move the mill indoors

activities.prompt: Arrange from the vehicle that wastes most energy on friction and air resistance to the one that would waste least.
items: A loaded cart dragged along the ground without wheels
A lorry on wheels on a tarred road
A streamlined train on steel rails
A maglev train floating above its guideway
A maglev pod inside a tube with the air pumped out

activities.definition: A force that opposes motion when two surfaces rub together.
distractors: A force that pulls all objects towards the Earth
The push between two like magnetic poles

glossary.definition: A force that opposes motion when two surfaces rub together.
Air resistance: a force that opposes the motion of an object through air.
Shaped so that air or water flows past easily.
To push away; like magnetic poles repel each other.
Magnetic levitation: using magnets to lift a vehicle above its track.
